source: Wan & Mei (2025) LLMs as Computable Approximations to Solomonoff Induction (re-read, experiment section)
finding: The only empirical test is few-shot example selection: pick the examples the model assigns lowest probability to the correct label (low confidence) versus highest. Low-confidence wins in every cell read. There is no test of Solomonoff-style predictions such as regret against a universal mixture.
numbers: 10 few-shot examples; Qwen2.5 3B/7B and Llama 3.1 8B / 3.2 3B, instruct versions; SMS, Emotion (6 class), AG News. SMS high vs low confidence: Qwen 3B 76.62 vs 90.07; Qwen 7B 92.73 vs 94.60; Llama 3.2 3B 64.94 vs 73.22; Llama 3.1 8B 85.22 vs 85.56. Emotion: Qwen 3B 55.21 vs 56.03; Qwen 7B 57.58 vs 57.68; Llama 3.2 3B 36.40 vs 41.86; Llama 3.1 8B 52.98 vs 53.22. AG News columns are garbled in the text layer (values 71.38 to 80.35 seen, not assigned).
limits: Gain is large only for the smallest models and near zero (0.1 to 0.4 points) for 7-8B. No random-selection baseline, no seeds or variance in the table, no other active-selection rule compared. The numbers do not separate the Solomonoff framing from ordinary hard-example selection. Table cell assignment read from a scrambled text layer.
agent_relevance: Do not cite Wan & Mei as evidence that the agent approximates Solomonoff induction. The usable item is cheap: choose few-shot demos the model finds surprising. Gap 5 stays open on the Solomonoff side (c19 is the only quantitative test, and it is negative).

source: Sun & Saparov (2025) Do Language Models Follow Occam's Razor? (full text re-read)
finding: Quality metric q(H) is the ratio of how often hypotheses appear in valid proofs to how often they appear in the shortest proof, so it is a proof-length proxy for parsimony. Reasoning prompts help (buffer-of-thought beats chain of thought; in-distribution demos help a little) but do not close the gap between weak and strong accuracy.
numbers: 100 i.i.d. examples per configuration; 95% CIs; heights 1-4. Height 1: all models above 80% (weak and strong). Multi-hypothesis: accuracy drops from above 80% to below 50% from height 1 to 2 (ground-truth hypotheses only 3.0 to 3.5), except GPT-4o. Height 4: weak accuracy at least 20%, strong accuracy and quality extremely low. 8 demos: in-distribution slightly better; out-of-distribution no significant gain. SFT on Qwen3-4B raises strong accuracy by +11.0 (h1), +8.5 (h2), +4.0 (h3), +1.5 (h4).
limits: Synthetic first-order-logic ontologies only. No arm that says in plain words 'give the simplest hypothesis' was found in the text; the prompts tested are reasoning-style (CoT, BoT), so the question whether a parsimony instruction closes the gap is still unanswered. Single paper; no replication found.
agent_relevance: The failure is not fixed by generic reasoning prompts. A parsimony step must be tested directly with a computable proxy such as proof or rule length, not left to the model's own sense of simple.

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi, Schwartz (2025/2026) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: Within one question, the shortest sampled reasoning chain is more often correct than a random or the longest one. This is trace length as a correctness signal, the closest 2025 LLM analogue of 'shorter description wins'.
numbers: Math-average accuracy (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, HMMT), shortest / random / longest: LN-Super-49B 63.4 / 47.7 / 28.9; R1-Distill-32B 60.0 / 55.5 / 37.8; QwQ-32B 71.1 / 68.9 / 56.7; R1-670B 83.3 / 78.2 / 58.9. Shortest chains use 31-48% fewer thinking tokens; longest use up to 75% more. Gap shortest vs longest up to 34.5 points. Temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95. GPQA-D, LN-Super-49B: 69.1 / 65.1 / 57.6.
limits: Comparison is within a question across several samples, so it needs k samples. Unfinished chains were excluded (they often loop), which flatters the shortest. Reasoning models on competition math and GPQA, not rule induction. Authors note harder questions still need long reasoning. Correlational; forcing short chains is a separate fine-tuning test.
agent_relevance: Cheap length proxy that works at the trace level. Test: among k sampled solutions, prefer the shortest consistent one, at equal total tokens.

source: Hassid et al. (2025/2026) short-m@k selection and fine-tuning on short chains (same paper, method and results sections)
finding: short-m@k runs k chains in parallel, stops when the first m finish, then majority-votes among those m. short-1@k beats majority@k at low compute; short-3@k beats majority@k at the budgets measured. Fine-tuning on short chains beats fine-tuning on random or long chains.
numbers: Compute counted as total thinking tokens. Abstract figures: short-1@k uses up to 40% fewer thinking tokens than majority voting at similar or better accuracy (LN-Super-49B); short-3@k consistently surpasses majority voting, up to 33% wall-time reduction. QwQ-32B showed a small decline for short-1@k at larger sample sizes. Models: LN-Super-49B, R1-32B, QwQ-32B, R1-670B.
limits: Equal-compute comparison against majority vote exists here, but for length of trace, not length of the rule. Not tested on ARC rule selection. Curve margins were not read as tables; only abstract numbers are exact.
agent_relevance: Partly informs gap 3 by analogy: a length-based selector can beat plain voting at equal tokens. It does not show that an MDL score over candidate programs does.

source: Wang, McCoy, Steinert-Threlkeld (2024) Minimization of Boolean Complexity in In-Context Concept Learning
finding: LLM in-context accuracy on numerical concepts falls as the concept's minimal description length (operator count in a small logical grammar) rises, mirroring Feldman 2000 in humans.
numbers: Complexity classes 1 to 5, 18 sampled concepts per class, 10 positive and 10 negative examples per prompt, 500 true and 500 false test prompts per accuracy point. Pearson r between complexity and class-mean accuracy: Gemma-2-9B -0.961 (p=0.009), Gemma-2-27B -0.898 (p=0.038), Qwen2-7B -0.884 (p=0.046), Qwen2-72B -0.854 (p=0.065, not significant). Qwen2-72B 90% to 74% from class 1 to 5; Gemma-2-9B 83% to 66%.
limits: Correlations are over 5 class means, so p-values rest on n=5. Only 4 open models, one grammar, one domain (numbers), preprint. The accuracy drop may reflect a larger space of rules, not a bias toward the shortest rule. No test of which rule the model outputs when two fit.
agent_relevance: Gives a grammar-relative length (operator count) that predicts LLM difficulty. Supports a small fixed DSL for the schema's rule length; does not show the model prefers short rules by choice.

source: Feldman (2000) Minimization of Boolean complexity in human concept learning, Nature 407:630-633 (abstract opened via PubMed)
finding: Subjective difficulty of a Boolean concept is directly proportional to its Boolean complexity, the length of the shortest logically equivalent propositional formula.
numbers: 41 mathematically distinct concept types in six families, a wider range than earlier studies. Participant counts and the exact correlation are not in the abstract; full text not opened.
limits: Abstract only. Later work disputes the generality (see d07). Complexity is relative to the logical basis (AND/OR/NOT).
agent_relevance: Founding human evidence that the shortest logical rule predicts how hard a concept is. It is difficulty, not human choice of rule.

source: Vigo (2013) The GIST of concepts, Cognition 129:138-162 (abstract opened via PubMed); Vigo (2006) note and Lafond et al. (2007) known only from search snippets
finding: A rival theory (GIST, invariance detection) is said to predict learning difficulty better than complexity-reduction models, including minimal description length, number of mental models, structural invariance and algebraic complexity, and than similarity models GCM, ALCOVE and SUSTAIN. Three experiments are reported.
numbers: No effect sizes in the abstract. Search snippets (not opened) say Vigo 2006 found some Feldman complexity values wrong and that the minimal-formula measure misses the canonical SHJ difficulty order; Lafond et al. 2007 reports evidence for non-minimal rules (title only, unverified).
limits: Written by the rival theory's proponent, so not an independent replication. The Lafond 2007 and Vigo 2006 pages were blocked by a bot check, so no numbers. Treat 'minimal formula fails SHJ' as reported, not checked.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the shortest rule is what humans use; the difficulty law has live competitors. Gap 8 stays partly open (full text of Feldman 2000 and Lafond 2007 needed).

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models, ICLR 2024
finding: On a 100-problem ARC subset with GPT-4, writing explicit hypotheses then programs beats direct prompting; having the LLM summarise 64 hypotheses to 8 helps further, a mild filter toward fewer, more general rules.
numbers: ARC (100 random problems): direct prompting 17%; program only 23%; summarised hypotheses 30%; human-selected from LLM candidates 33%. 28 of the 30 tasks solved with summaries already had a correct hypothesis before summarising. 1D-ARC: direct 39.6 vs program only 61.1. SyGuS: 94.3% with 8 programs.
limits: Compute is not equalised: the pipeline samples 64 hypotheses and 8 programs per task against one direct answer. Summaries can be vague and sometimes drop the correct hypothesis. No arm selects by rule length, so it does not test shortest-rule selection.
agent_relevance: A propose, then verify on all examples, then filter loop works on rule-induction items. The missing control is the equal-token one the critique asks for (gap 1).

source: Singhal, Mishra, Malach, Galanti (2026) LLM Priors for ERM over Programs (LLM-PV), ICML 2026
finding: An LLM proposes candidate programs; they are executed and the one with lowest held-out validation error is chosen. Selection uses validation error, not program length, though the theory is length-bounded ERM (Occam-style sample bounds).
numbers: Trained on 200 examples at length n=10, tested up to n=100. LLM-PV reaches 100% test accuracy with 200 examples on 10-parity, CAP and IsPrime, where SGD-trained and fine-tuned models stay near chance (about 50%) even with 100k examples. Test set 10,000 examples; validation set 100.
limits: Synthetic algorithmic tasks; hand-chosen program class. No length-ranked arm, so it cannot say whether length adds anything beyond validation error. The paper says selected programs are often compact but gives no ablation.
agent_relevance: Held-out validation error is a strong ranker; any length proxy must be shown to add to it. Supports 'verify on held-out examples' as the main step, with length as tiebreak.

source: Greenblatt (2024) Getting 50% (SoTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o (Redwood blog; known from a search summary, page not opened)
finding: About 8,000 Python programs sampled per problem, filtered to those passing all example pairs, then majority vote picks the 3 submissions. Program length is not the selection criterion.
numbers: Roughly 50% reported on an ARC-AGI-1 subset (from search summary; not re-read).
limits: Search summary only; not opened this session.
agent_relevance: The standard ARC LLM baseline for gap 3 is filter-then-vote; no published equal-token MDL-vs-vote number was found. Gap 3 stays open.

source: Zenil et al. (2018) A Decomposition Method for Global Evaluation of Shannon Entropy and Local Estimations of Algorithmic Complexity (BDM paper, theorem statements)
finding: States the Coding Theorem (|-log2 m(s) - K(s)| < c) and the Invariance Theorem, defines CTM and BDM, proves BDM(X) bounds K(X) up to additive terms, and states BDM behaves like Shannon entropy when it loses accuracy.
numbers: BDM(s,l,m) = sum of CTM(block) + log(multiplicity). Proposition 4.1 gives K(X) <= BDM(X) + O(log^2 |A|) plus an error term, and an upper bound on BDM in terms of the adjacency-set size times K(X) plus O(n log n). Worked example 57.566 bits for a string with two repeated blocks (26.99 bits each).
limits: Secondary statement of the founding theorems, not Solomonoff 1964, Kolmogorov 1965, Chaitin 1966 or Levin 1973 themselves, which were not opened. Authors are the method's proponents.
agent_relevance: For short rules CTM or BDM is the principled length measure, but the machine space is still a choice. Founding theorems are known here only through secondary texts.

source: arXiv 2601.05280 Large Language Models As Shannon Lossy Compressors Not Solomonoff Induction Estimators (search snippet only)
finding: Search summary says CTM tables cover only small objects, BDM splits larger ones, estimates depend on the chosen machine space and so are not universal in practice, and CTM-style statistics are weak tests of Solomonoff-like induction.
numbers: No new numbers; see c19 for the verified 26-checkpoint result.
limits: Snippet only; a separate 2023-2024 critique paper of BDM bias was not found.
agent_relevance: Keeps K04 and K18 as stated. No independent 2020-2026 critique of the coding-theorem method was located.

source: Sterkenburg (2026) Solomonoff induction, arXiv 2603.20274 (search snippet only)
finding: Search summary says the chapter discusses tension between computability desiderata for universal predictors and dependence on the reference machine.
agent_relevance: Philosophical background for the machine-dependence caveat (K01).

source: Negative search result for gap 3: MDL ranking of LLM-sampled programs vs majority vote on ARC (MADIL arXiv 2505.01081 is the nearest)
finding: No paper found that ranks LLM-sampled candidate programs by description length and compares with majority vote or self-consistency at equal tokens on ARC. MADIL uses MDL as a search criterion inside its own DSL, not as a ranker over LLM samples.
numbers: MADIL 7% on ARC Prize 2024 private set (from earlier evidence c18). Nothing new.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search: arXiv search API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors during this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 is open. The honest test is one we must run.

source: Negative search result for gap 6: description-language invariance in practice
finding: No study located that re-ranks the same candidate rules in natural language, Python and a DSL and reports rank change. Closest are d05 (one grammar fixed) and d02 (proof length in one FOL).
limits: Search tools were rate-limited; this is a gap in what was found, not proof none exists.
agent_relevance: Run the schema's own K01 test: rank by two phrasings and report Spearman rho.

source: Synthesis for gap 2: length proxies on file (d02 proof length, d03 trace tokens, d05 operator count, d09 validation error)
finding: Each proxy tracks correctness in its own setting: proof-based quality q(H) (d02), reasoning-trace tokens (d03, shortest best), operator count in a grammar (d05, accuracy falls with length), held-out validation error (d09, selects exact rules). No study compares them on one item set against held-out correctness.
numbers: Trace length: shortest vs longest 63.4 vs 28.9 average accuracy (LN-Super-49B, d03). Operator-count class 1 to 5: r from -0.85 to -0.96 (d05, n=5 means).
limits: Different tasks and models; the numbers are not comparable across rows. Synthesis line, nothing new opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open as a head-to-head. Interim order: held-out validation error first (d09), trace length as cheap second (d03).
